sources.title: Akiko Yosano (Q464104), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): English label 'Akiko Yosano', description 'Japanese tanka poet (1878-1942)', Korean label 요사노 아키코, born 7 December 1878, died 29 May 1942, citizenship Japan. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'YOSANO Akiko', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (biographical note by library staff, English and Japanese texts read from the site's published data): poet; graduate of Sakai Girls' School; joined the Kansai Seinen Bungakukai in 1899 and the Tokyo Shinshisha in 1900; published tanka in the magazine Myojo; published Midaregami in August 1901, which created a great sensation; went on to publish many collections as a representative of Japanese Romanticism; translated Genji Monogatari into modern Japanese, helped found the Bunka Gakuin in 1921, and made constructive statements on problems of women and education. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: neutral national-library reference note; used for the career chronology.

Poetry Foundation, 'Yosano Akiko' (poet biography), read in full: one of the best-known female poets from post-classical Japan; Midaregami (Tangled Hair, 1901) created a stir for its frank depiction of female passion and, in tanka form, defied the conventions of traditional verse by setting religious and spiritual metaphors against sensuous description; the journal Myojo first published her work; when it folded her writing became the primary income of her family; a year in France in 1912, then the translation of the Tale of Genji; more than 20 collections of poetry and numerous volumes of social criticism; established the Bunka Gakuin in 1921; the English translations and Janine Beichman's 2002 study are listed. Poetry-world institution; admiring in tone; some details (a 'women's trade school') differ from other sources.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yosano Akiko' (encyclopaedia biography by the editors), read in full: poet whose new style caused a sensation in Japanese literary circles; interested in poetry from school, published a private poetry magazine with friends; joined Yosano Tekkan's Shinshisha in 1900 and contributed to Myojo; Midaregami (1901) brought her fame, Yume no hana (1906) revealed her developing art; a year in France from 1912 and the collection Natsu yori aki e (1914); on returning she began translating Genji monogatari into modern Japanese; established the Bunka Gakuin in 1921 where she also taught, and later wrote literary criticism; the posthumous collection Hakuoshu (1942). Neutral encyclopaedia entry.

Christopher Harding, 'Yosano Akiko - a great of modern Japanese poetry', Engelsberg Ideas (21 February 2022), read in full: historian's portrait; Akiko first wrote poems at sixteen, partly (it was said) from concern about the quality of women's poetry; Midaregami (399 poems) was dismissed by one reviewer as the 'precocious prattle of a young girl' but found a ready readership among the young; she concluded the state school system produced loyal subjects with stunted imaginations and co-founded the Bunkagakuin (1921), where she wrote a literature textbook meant to inspire love of poetry and prose and taught the Tale of Genji; she disagreed with feminists who stressed state support for motherhood; the article also covers her anti-war poem of 1904 and a late nationalist turn, which are context and are not scored here. Independent historian's essay; includes critical voices (a hostile reviewer, socialists who disliked the anti-war poem, admirers puzzled by her later outlook).

Gaye Rowley, 'Yosano Akiko and The Tale of Genji' (author's book page, University of Michigan Center for Japanese Studies, 2000; revised open-access edition 2022) with the Fulcrum open-access abstract, read: scholar's summary that a major part of Akiko's career was devoted to the Japanese classics, above all Genji; she wrote biographical studies of Murasaki Shikibu, series of lectures on Genji and a scholarly edition of the text; for fourteen years between 1909 and 1923 she worked on a Genji commentary that, just short of completion, was destroyed in the fires after the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1 September 1923; her two colloquial translations are Shin'yaku Genji monogatari (abridged, 1912-13) and Shin-shin'yaku Genji monogatari (complete, 1938-39), both still in print; the abstract says she modernized the tale as a novel and pioneered academic research on it, and that 'poetess of passion' no longer captures her career. The full open-access text could not be downloaded in this session (automated download returned 403), so only the author's summary and the publisher abstract were read, not the book. Scholarly specialist; the abstract's claims of pioneering are the author's thesis.

Ohio State University Libraries Japanese Collections blog, 'A Rare Acquisition: Yosano Akiko's A New Translation of The Tale of Genji' (23 March 2025), read in full: the library's Rare Books and Manuscripts holding of the 1912 first edition of Shin'yaku Genji monogatari in four books with sixty-one woodblock prints by Nakazawa Hiromitsu; describes it as transforming Genji into a modern-language work and an intervention at a time when it was studied through a male-centric academic lens; says a Yomiuri newspaper once called her a 'modern Murasaki Shikibu'; lists later modern-Japanese translators of Genji. Library collection blog; admiring and brief.

Sakai City (Osaka Prefecture), 'Yosano Akiko' historic-figures page (English), read in full (last updated 2025): born in 1878 into the Surugaya confectionery family in Kaino-cho, Sakai; composed tanka in the Meiji, Taisho and Showa periods and was called the 'Poetess of Passion'; Midare-gami (1901) was popular with the younger generation and is regarded as a Romanticism masterpiece; translated classics including the Tale of Genji into modern Japanese; wrote many essays on women's rights and played an active role in women's education. Civic hometown page; promotional in tone.

Setsuko Shoji (Ichimura Gakuen Junior College), 'A Historical Study of Akiko Yosano's Ideas on Physical Education' (KAKEN research-project abstract, 1985-86, report published 1987), read in full: scholarly abstract stating that her educational ideas rested on humanitarian educational thought and a liberal approach that questioned competing to win; that she criticized a military drill proposed by a special meeting on physical education; that she rejected interference by the authorities in physical-education methods (linked to Bunka Gakuin, though the abstract's wording is unclear); and that the researcher sees a 'blind spot' in her liberal thinking in her later acceptance of Japan's wartime aggression (political context, not scored). Short funding abstract by an independent education historian; the Bunka Gakuin link is not clearly worded.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_yosano_poetryfound, src_yosano_britannica, src_yosano_harding, src_yosano_ndl, src_yosano_rowley | 1901-1914 | poetry-world institution, encyclopaedia, historian's essay, national-library note, scholar's summary] The Poetry Foundation says Midaregami defied conventions of traditional Japanese verse by setting religious and spiritual metaphors against sensuous description; Britannica says the freshness and unconventionality of her poetry had already attracted attention and that Midaregami brought her fame; Harding describes her use of a thousand-year-old form to speak of young women's lives and notes that a hostile reviewer still found it 'precocious prattle' while young readers took it up; NDL calls it a great sensation and places her as a representative of Japanese Romanticism. Rowley's abstract adds that she modernized the Tale of Genji as a novel. Four independent writers agree that the work broke with convention, including one that records hostile reception, but the evidence is about the reception and character of the work rather than about her creative process, so the claim is a strong inference. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed and kept; independently corroborated across institutional, encyclopaedic and historian sources. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): creative_originality lowered from 80 / 0.66 to 76 / 0.6 because poetry-world institution, encyclopedia and a historian carry the praise, retrospectively.

persistence.rationale: [src_yosano_rowley, src_yosano_poetryfound, src_yosano_osu, src_yosano_britannica | 1909-1939 | scholar's summary, poetry-world institution, library blog, encyclopaedia] Rowley's summary states that she worked fourteen years (1909-1923) on a Genji commentary that was destroyed just short of completion in the fires after the Great Kanto Earthquake, and that she nevertheless produced an abridged colloquial translation (1912-13) and a complete one (1938-39); Britannica says she began the translation after returning from France in 1912, and the Poetry Foundation counts more than 20 collections of poetry and numerous volumes of social criticism. The long continuation of the Genji project across a major loss is documented only through one scholar's publicity summary (the book itself could not be opened), and the sources do not say how she responded to the fire in her own words, so the row is a moderate lean at moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 80 / 0.64 to 74 / 0.55 because the fourteen-year commentary and its loss rest on a single scholar's summary page and the book text was not read.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_yosano_rowley, src_yosano_osu, src_yosano_harding | 1909-1939 | scholar's summary, library blog, historian's essay] Rowley's summary says that alongside poetry a major part of her career was devoted to the Japanese classics: biographical studies of Murasaki Shikibu, series of lectures on Genji, a scholarly edition of the text and two translations, and that she had read Genji many times before she was twenty; Harding says she taught Genji at her school; the Ohio State blog describes the 1912 translation as both a scholarly achievement and an intervention at a time when the text was studied through a male-centric academic lens. The commitment to one classic over three decades is well attested; judgments of the scholarship's quality come from the author-scholar and an admiring library blog, hence moderate confidence.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_yosano_ndl, src_yosano_britannica, src_yosano_poetryfound, src_yosano_rowley, src_yosano_harding | 1901-1942 | national-library note, encyclopaedia, poetry-world institution, scholar's summary, historian's essay] The sources place her in tanka poetry, translation of a classical novel into modern Japanese, scholarly work and lecturing on Genji, literary criticism, social criticism, school founding and teaching, and a literature textbook; NDL says she was active in a wide range of fields beyond tanka. The range is real and multiply sourced but largely literary and educational, and one of the sources is promotional, so the score is moderate-high with moderate confidence.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_yosano_poetryfound, src_yosano_harding, src_yosano_kaken_pe | 1901-1930s | poetry-world institution, historian's essay, scholarly abstract] Poetry and education only: the Poetry Foundation says Midaregami defied the conventions of traditional verse; Harding says she judged the state school system capable of little but producing loyal subjects, co-founded a school that gave the arts prominence and wrote a literature textbook aimed at love of poetry rather than the utilitarian values of the day; the KAKEN abstract says she criticized a proposed military drill in physical education and rejected authorities' interference in teaching methods, and favoured a questioning of competing to win. Her stands on war, nationalism and the state are context and are deliberately not scored. The documented pattern is a consistent preference for her own judgment in literary form and teaching, but the education claims come from an essay and a one-paragraph funding abstract, so the row is an inference.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_yosano_harding, src_yosano_poetryfound, src_yosano_kaken_pe | 1901-1930s | historian's essay, poetry-world institution, scholarly abstract] Harding reports that a reviewer dismissed Midaregami as 'precocious prattle' and that, as with that book, criticism seems to have done little to shake her convictions or harm her reputation; the Poetry Foundation notes the stir the book created; the KAKEN abstract says she rejected authorities' interference in teaching methods. Harding's 'seems to' is a historian's reading, a good part of his example concerns a political poem that is not scored, and there is no source showing how she answered critics face to face, so the row is a moderate lean with low confidence. Impact is dual-edged because the same firmness appears in the scholarly abstract's remark about blind spots in her thinking.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_yosano_ndl, src_yosano_britannica, src_yosano_harding, src_yosano_poetryfound | 1899-1921 | national-library note, encyclopaedia, historian's essay, poetry-world institution] The sources say she joined the Kansai Seinen Bungakukai in 1899 and Tekkan's Tokyo Shinshisha in 1900 and contributed to Myojo, and that in 1921 she helped found and teach at the Bunka Gakuin; Harding says she took up the school project out of concern about what state schools taught. The co-founding and the move into poetry circles are well attested, but the sources do not describe her own part in organising the school (Britannica and the Poetry Foundation say 'established', NDL says 'helped found'), so the row reflects participation in starting things rather than leadership of them.

portrait.source: Portrait photograph of Yosano Akiko, photographer unknown, taken before her death in 1942 and published in the poetry collection Yosano Akiko shiikashu (Sogensha, Tokyo, 1952), as reproduced in the National Diet Library's digital exhibition 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures' (entry for YOSANO Akiko, source item NDL Digital Collections pid 1341526). The library's entry names the sitter. The file is the library's published exhibition image (810 x 1101 pixels) with no resizing, cropping or upscaling; it is a halftone book reproduction.
portrait.license: Public domain (declared by the National Diet Library for all images in 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures'; the anonymous photograph was published in Japan in 1952 or earlier, so its term under the 1899 Copyright Act had expired by 1970)
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown, published 1952 in Yosano Akiko shiikashu (Sogensha). Source: Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures, National Diet Library, Japan (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/)
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / RESOLVED WITH THE LEAD ROUTE (NDL Portraits exhibition) BUT THE SOURCE BOOK IS A 1952 PUBLICATION, NOT 1942: the lead named 'Yosano Akiko Shiikashu, by 1942'; the holder's item data show that book is Yosano Akiko shiikashu (Sogen Senso 223, Sogensha, Tokyo, 1952, NDL pid 1341526), and the exhibition's other photographs come from Nihon bungaku album vol. 16 (Chikuma Shobo, 1955, pid 1336287). HOLDER RECORD CHECKED: the NDL exhibition entry (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/347/index.html, its site data read) lists seven photographs of the sitter and names these two books; the NDL Digital Collections item API for pid 1341526 confirms title, publisher and year 1952, the exhibition name 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures: Yosano Akiko', and permission type 'ooc' (item not restricted); the exhibition's terms page (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/about) states that all images used in the digital exhibition are in the public domain. No holder contradiction found. RIGHTS BASIS (independent of the library's declaration): the photograph is an anonymous photograph of the sitter who died in 1942 (so taken by 1942) and was published in Japan in 1952 at the latest; under Article 23 of the 1899 Copyright Act and Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the 1970 Act, a photograph first published in Japan before 1 January 1958 has expired in Japan (term 10 years from publication) by 1970 and so was not restored by the URAA in 1996 (this reading follows the Wikimedia Commons PD-Japan-oldphoto licence text, which I read; it is a legal reading, not a statement by the holder). CAVEATS: the photographer is unknown; the book captions were not read (the book viewer is not exposed through the exhibition page), so the link between the exhibition image and the 1952 book rests on the library's data; I did not open Commons file 'YOSANO Akiko.jpg' as the source of the file, only its wikitext, which cites the same 1952 book (author unknown, date 'by 1942'); a second Commons file 'Akiko Yosano.jpg' (from a 1933-34 history book) is only 348 x 544 pixels and its page says only 'The contributor has this source', so it was not used. The image used is exhibition image 0347_1.jpg (810 x 1101) with no resizing, no cropping and no upscaling; kind likeness (a photograph of the sitter in her lifetime). ZERO POLITICS: primary identity is tanka poet, translator and teacher; the sources also describe feminist activism, an anti-war poem (1904) and later nationalist writing, none of which is scored or carded (impact domains literary, cultural, educational). ATTRIBUTION: attributable (many dated, documented works and institutions); attribution_confirmed true. VOCABULARY: occupations poet, writer, teacher; fields literature, education; tags nonconformist, prolific; archetype creative_creator; all labelled in en.ts and ko.ts (checked); the occupations translator, critic and educator have no labels and are not used. KO NAME: Wikidata Korean label 요사노 아키코. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: National Diet Library Portraits biography (src_yosano_ndl) together with Britannica. READ (9 sources incl. Wikidata): NDL note (English and Japanese from the exhibition database), Poetry Foundation, Britannica, Harding (Engelsberg Ideas), Rowley book page plus Fulcrum abstract, Ohio State library blog, Sakai City page, KAKEN physical-education abstract; KAKEN abstract on Bunka Gakuin's founding (Nishimura Isaku) was read for context but not cited. PERSPECTIVES: national library, poetry institution, encyclopaedia, independent historian (counter-voices: hostile reviewer, socialists, puzzled admirers), Genji scholar, library-collection blog, hometown civic page, education-history scholar. NOT OPENED: Rowley's book text (the open-access PDF returned HTTP 403 to an automated download and was not retrieved by other means), Beichman's Embracing the Firebird (lending only), Japan Times articles by Pulvers (2009) and Sato (2002) (paywalled; only the teaser was visible, so they are not cited), Wikipedia (orientation only), her own poems and essays (self-report; not used for any row). Sources disagree on the Bunka Gakuin (Poetry Foundation calls it a women's trade school, Britannica a school for girls, Harding a school where the arts were prominent) and on what the 1923 fire destroyed (Rowley: a commentary; a Japan Times teaser: a complete translation); the cards avoid both disputes. EXCLUSIONS: family and marriage details, number of children, the 1928 Manchuria trip and later wartime poems are not scored. SPARSE PROFILE: 7 rows, scores 62-80, confidence 0.45-0.66. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk rows reviewed: persistence (80/0.64 lowered to 74/0.55: key fact rests on one scholar's summary page), creative_originality (kept: four independent perspectives incl. a hostile reviewer), independent_thinking (kept at 72/0.52: already limited to poetry and education, politics excluded).
